stt: Ask HN: Which DRM-free ebook reader to buy?
x:
I've been using a Kobo for around a year now.

Plusses:

* They're cheaper than Kindle to buy

* The Kobo store is well stocked and competitively priced

* You can upload your own books easily by dragging and dropping the files as if it's a thumb drive or by using Calibre (see calibre-ebook.com).

* The screen looks just as good as my partner's Kindle.

stt: Ask HN: Do you still buy physical tech books like “Learn Rust” or “Learn Go”?
x:
Completely switched to eBooks. Main reason is space and also availability.
I move often and if I had all or most books that I read in paper form, it would both take too much space and be problem to move to other place.
I don't miss paper books. I read fiction on eBook reader (first Kindle, but switched to Kobo for bigger screen) and for me, feeling is same as with paper to extent that sometimes when dust or hair drops on screen I move it away before turning page as I would do with paper book so it doesn't stay between pages.
IT books I read on my computer. For them I prefer eBook format as it is easier and faster to navigate, you can do text search, copy from them etc.

Saving few trees from being converted to paper is also a motivation :)

I don't think that's true for most people, but for me the difference isn't large enough to matter.

It probably takes most people 1 or 2 minutes to click the one click buy button on Amazon and download a book. I can get a book from Z-Library on telegram, upload it to Dropbox, and have it downloaded to my Kobo in 3-4 minutes -- not a big deal on book reading time scales.

It's not just Amazon. Kobo has gone Adobe corrupted too and now instead of epub downloads, or even just the basic consideration of telling you what format the book is in you first have to pay for the book then you get to find out weather you're getting actual text or just some shell of a drm file pointing to adobe's servers (.acsm).

I've had to sit through a couple 30 minute chat holds with Kobo in order to get refunds recently due to their lack of proper labeling.

When there is no option to buy the actual text of a book I will try pirating and it is almost always simpler and faster. If pirating fails too then I have to find an old paperback to buy and send off to a scanner/OCR company.

stt: It's easier and faster to pirate an e-book, than it is to buy it
x: Got tired of giving Amazon and other big advertising companies my reading list to profile me with. Bought an Android-based eReader. Found it incredibly difficult to find most books off of Amazon. Even harder to find books without DRM. Also never found a satisfactory way to sync book progress between devices (phone and eReader). Eventually gave up and bought a Rakuten Kobo. Comes with DRM and probably sells my data to third parties. Has poor support for books in languages I read. But has a book store with a halfway decent selection of mainstream books and at least I'm not giving my data directly to Amazon. Honestly wondering when Apple is going to come out with a sexy eInk device.

Try to buy a kobo and connect with your getpocket (firefox read it later).

I cannot read blog posts on my computer but I can read this way.

It has a very nice feature. You read the articles offline (after you sync the kobo with pocket), and when you click on the blog links, it presents you with the option of connect to the internet or store the link in pocket. That way you can read the link later and focus on the blog post
